units.title: A Disciplined Young Person
units.intro: This unit is about **self-control**: controlling your emotions, words, actions and desires. It also shows why **honesty** is the best policy.

pins.text: determination and commitment to reach our goals

ways.title: What students do to show self-control

pins.text: "I strictly follow my plans and tasks."
"I behave, even when no one is looking."

cards.title: What is self-control?
body: **Self-control** is the ability to control our **emotions**, **words**, **actions** and **desires**.
It is also showing **determination** and **commitment** to reach our goals.

cards.title: Four things we control
body: Tap the dots. What do we control?

cards.title: Memory trick: E-W-A-D
body: **E**very **W**ise **A**ct **D**elays: think first, then act.

cards.title: How students show self-control
body: Four students tell us what they do. Tap the dots.

cards.title: When do we need it?
body: Some things make us **angry**. Some things are hard to accept.
Example: you must pick one of two choices. You are not sure. You feel **irritated**.
Then control your emotions. **Think before** you decide.

cards.title: Stop, think, then act
body: Self-control = controlling your emotions and **avoiding quick actions**.
When you want to control your emotions, say what you want to do in a **soft and low voice**.

cards.title: An example
body: A student sits with his homework. He says: "I will play **after** I finish my homework."
He controls his desire to play. He follows his plan.

cards.q: Your friend makes you angry. What shows self-control?

options.A: Shout at your friend at once
options.B: Think first and speak in a soft, low voice

cards.why: The textbook says: control your emotions, think before you decide, and speak in a soft and low voice (p. 2).

cards.title: The library incident (a drama)
body: Rahel and Hagos talk **loudly** in the school library. They disturb other students.
**Semira** is angry. She crosses her arms and shouts at them.
**Rahel** answers with pride: "Mind your own reading."
Semira stands up and comes close to Rahel with wide eyes.

cards.title: Who is who?
body: Tap each person.

cards.title: Watch each person

states.label: Semira
states.text: **Semira** is right about the rule: read quietly in the library. But she shouts and comes close to Rahel. She does **not** control her anger.

states.label: Rahel
states.text: **Rahel** answers with pride and calls Semira a nagging person. She does **not** control her words.

states.label: Hagos
states.text: **Hagos** speaks **calmly**. He says: "We were wrong to talk loudly." He also says Semira should have told them **politely**. He shows **self-control**.

states.label: Librarian
states.text: The **librarian** comes. He says: "You are not supposed to argue inside the library." He sends the three students out.

body: Move the slider.

cards.title: What the drama teaches
body: Hagos stayed calm and said sorry for his mistake.
Semira was right about the rule, but she was wrong to shout. She **should have told them politely**.
The library belongs to all of us. We are **all responsible** to follow its rules.

cards.title: What would you do? (Exercise 1.1)
body: The textbook asks you to think about hard situations:
- Friends offer you a **cigarette**. Smoking is very dangerous and can kill you.
- Your teacher says "go back to class", but you have a permission slip.
- You broke your neighbour's new **jebena**. No one saw you.
- You want to study, but friends want you to play.
Think: which answer shows **self-control**?

cards.q: Friends offer you a cigarette. They say: "Smoke or stay away from us." Which answer shows self-control?

options.A: Try one puff, then throw it away
options.B: Take it and throw it away secretly
options.C: Say "no" and warn them of the dangers

cards.why: The textbook says smoking is very dangerous and can kill you (p. 3). Saying "no" controls your desire to please your friends.

cards.q: You broke your neighbour's jebena. No one saw you. Which answer is honest?

options.A: Leave it there and tell nobody
options.B: Throw it away before anyone sees
options.C: Go to the neighbour, tell calmly what happened and say sorry
options.D: Ask your parents to buy a new one secretly

cards.why: A good student says "I'm sorry" when he makes a mistake and tells the truth every time (p. 15).

cards.title: A hole in the fence (a story)
body: A little boy had a **bad temper**.
His father gave him a bag of **nails**. Each time he lost his temper, he had to hammer nails into the fence.
On the first day he drove **38 nails** into the fence.

cards.title: The fence, day by day

states.label: First day
states.text: **38 nails** on the first day. The boy loses his temper again and again.

states.label: Weeks later
states.text: He learns to control his anger. The number of nails gets **smaller**. Holding his temper is **easier** than driving nails.

states.label: Nails out
states.text: He does not lose his temper at all. Now he pulls out **one nail** for each good day. All the nails are gone, but the **holes** stay.

body: Move the slider.

cards.title: The father's lesson
body: The father said: "Look at the holes in the fence. The fence will never be the same."
When you say things in **anger**, they leave a **scar**, like these holes.
You can say "I'm sorry" many times, but the wound is still there.

cards.title: Words can hurt
body: A **verbal wound** (a wound made by words) is as bad as a physical one.
Our words are like **feathers**. Once they are released, we can never get them back.

cards.title: Friends are jewels
body: Friends and loved ones are very **rare jewels**.
They make you smile. They encourage you to succeed. They listen and praise you.
**Water your relationships with kindness**, and they will grow.

cards.title: Memory trick: the song
body: The song says: "Oh, be careful little **tongue** what you say... little **ears** what you hear... little **hands** what you touch... little **eyes** what you see."

cards.q: The boy drove 38 nails on the first day. Each time he lost his temper he hammered two nails. How many times did he lose his temper that day?
cards.why: Two nails for each time: 38 ÷ 2 = 19 times (p. 7).

cards.title: Winning trust and respect
body: Self-control is not only about words and emotions.
With self-control you learn to become:
- **respectful**, **patient**, **honest**,
- **thankful** and **forgiving**,
- wanted by your family, community and friends.
You also feel a **sense of accomplishment**.

cards.title: Memory trick: P-R-H-T-F
body: "**P**lease **R**espect **H**onest **T**eens **F**irst": five things self-control helps you become.

cards.title: The champion of polio
body: **Jonas Salk** invented the **polio vaccine**. It is used all over the world to prevent polio.
In Eritrea, the vaccine is given to children **under the age of five** every year.
He first tested it on **himself, his wife and his three sons**.

cards.title: Who was Jonas Salk?
body: He was born in **New York City** on 28 October **1914**.
His parents had no formal education, but they wanted their children to succeed.
He was the **first in his family** to go to college.
He wanted to study law, but he was also interested in medical science.

steps.text: Born in New York City in 1914.
At medical school he studied the **flu virus**. In 1939 World War II began. Experts feared a flu epidemic.
In 1947, after **eight long years** of work, he developed a vaccine against **polio**.
In **1955** he tested the vaccine in humans. It worked. It saved thousands of lives.
He died on 23 June **1995**. In his last years he searched for a vaccine against **AIDS**.

cards.title: Polio
body: Polio is a virus. It caused **paralysis** and sometimes **death**.

cards.title: He did not patent it
body: To **patent** a vaccine means to have the only right to use it and sell it.
Salk **refused** to patent his vaccine. He wanted the **whole world** to benefit, **for free**.
He was patient and controlled his emotions during long years of research.

cards.title: High moral values
body: A person with high self-control develops high **moral values**.
**Morals** are rules that help us behave in ways that are appropriate, caring and thoughtful of others and ourselves.
A person with moral values knows **right from wrong**. He makes choices that cause **no harm** to himself or others.

cards.title: Moral or immoral?
head: Moral values
Immoral values
rows: no harm to self or others
can lead to enemies and crime

cards.title: Growing up
body: As a child, your parents and teachers reminded you how to behave. ("Don't touch, it is hot!")
Now you are growing up. It is **your** job to keep yourself in control.
You should know right from wrong.

cards.title: What you do when no one is watching
body: Honest one day and dishonest the next? That is not self-control.
**Consistency** and self-control go hand in hand.
**Self-control is what you do when no one is watching.**

cards.title: The self-control circle

steps.text: **Beware of your thoughts**, because they affect your feelings.
**Control your feelings**, because they affect your decisions.
**Think of your decisions**, because they lead to actions.
**Control your actions**, because they can have serious consequences.

body: Tap the arrow to go round the circle.

cards.q: A person with high moral values...

options.A: makes choices that cause no harm to himself or others
options.B: behaves well only when adults are near

cards.why: A person with moral values distinguishes between right and wrong and makes choices that cause no harm (p. 11).

cards.title: The boy who cried "Hyena"
body: A young **shepherd** lived in a small village in Eritrea.
One day he was bored. He decided to play a **trick** on the villagers.

steps.text: He shouted: "Help! Hyena!" The villagers ran to help. There was no hyena. He laughed: "I fooled all of you."
A few days later he did the same trick again. The villagers were **very angry**.
Then a hyena **really** came and attacked the sheep. He shouted for help, but the villagers **laughed**. They thought it was another trick.
At last they came. The hyena was running away. **Many sheep were dead.**

cards.title: What happened because of his lies?
body: He showed little **respect** to his community.
He also **hurt himself**: he lost the **trust** of all the villagers.
Being disrespectful like the shepherd is a sure sign of a **lack of self-control**.

cards.title: "A Student Wanted!"
body: A newspaper, **Eritrea Profile**, looks for a good student. Some qualities:
- listens carefully and asks questions when he does not understand,
- respects the family, helps the elderly and the disabled,
- knows the nation's symbols (anthem, flag, currency),
- does not smoke cigarettes,
- keeps the environment clean,
- tells the truth every time.

cards.title: Three magic sentences
body: The wanted student says:
- "**I don't know**" when he does not know a thing,
- "**I'm sorry**" when he has made a mistake,
- "**I'll do it**" when he is asked to do a task.

cards.title: More qualities
body: - moves quickly and makes little noise,
- knows the cultures and traditions of the nation,
- is polite to every student,
- wants to learn different languages,
- loves animals and plants,
- likes to read good books,
- plays sports in the break instead of wasting it.

cards.title: Summary
body: Self-control is the **foundation of moral behaviour**.
It begins with controlling your **thoughts** and making positive, moral choices.
Key terms: **self-control, emotion, moral, value, desire**.

cards.q: Why did the villagers not help the shepherd when the hyena really came?

options.B: They thought it was another trick
options.D: They were afraid of the hyena

cards.why: He had lied two times, so they did not trust him any more (p. 13, 16).

tips.text: Learn the **definition** of self-control word by word: "the ability to control our emotions, words, actions and desires".
Remember the **circle**: thoughts → feelings → decisions → actions.
Exam trick: "Self-control is what you do when **no one is watching**."
For "what would you do?" questions, choose the answer that is **calm, honest and respectful**, and say why.
Know the stories and their lessons: the **fence** (words hurt), **Jonas Salk** (patience), the **shepherd** (lies lose trust).

questions.q: Which of the following is true about self-control?

options.A: It means not talking in class when the teacher is watching you.
options.B: It means taking actions without the instruction of your parents.
options.C: It means showing determination and commitment in achieving our goals.
options.D: It means never reacting when others bully you.

why: The textbook defines self-control as controlling emotions, words, actions and desires.
It also says it is **showing determination and commitment in achieving our goals** (p. 1).
questions.tip: Look for the words of the definition: "determination and commitment".

similar.q: Self-control is the ability to control our emotions, words, actions and ___.

questions.q: Which of the following is the result of self-control?

options.B: Getting good grades through whatever means
options.C: Helping others by setting an example yourself first

why: "Through whatever means" includes bad ways, like cheating. That is not self-control.
Self-control makes you respectful and wanted by others. Setting a good example helps others.
questions.tip: "Whatever means" is a warning sign: it allows wrong actions.

similar.q: Name one thing self-control helps you become.

questions.q: Lack of self-control can lead to:
why: Immoral values lead to behaviour that is disrespectful and even dangerous (p. 11).
A person with immoral values may engage in crime and have smoking and drinking habits.
So all of these can happen.
questions.tip: When every option is a bad result, "all of the above" is often right.

similar.q: Name two habits of a person with immoral values.

questions.q: What is self-control?
questions.answer: Self-control is the ability to control our emotions, words, actions and desires. It is also showing determination and commitment in achieving our goals.
why: Give the four things: emotions, words, actions, desires.
Add the second part: determination and commitment to reach goals.
questions.tip: Use E-W-A-D: Emotions, Words, Actions, Desires.

similar.q: Give one example of self-control from the students on p. 1.
similar.a: "I think before I act." (or: I follow my plans; I control my temper; I behave when no one is looking)

questions.q: Mention three benefits of self-control.
questions.answer: Any three: you become respectful, patient, honest, thankful, forgiving; you are wanted by family, community and friends; you feel a sense of accomplishment; you win trust and respect.
why: p. 9 lists what self-control helps you become.
Pick any three from the list.
questions.tip: Remember "Please Respect Honest Teens First".

similar.q: What feeling does a person with high self-control have?

questions.q: In what ways are self-control and moral values related?
questions.answer: A person with high self-control develops high moral values. Self-control is the foundation of moral behaviour: you stop and think whether your thoughts and feelings lead to actions that are morally correct.
why: p. 11: high self-control → high moral values.
p. 16: self-control is the foundation of moral behaviour.
questions.tip: Say the link in one sentence: more self-control → higher moral values.

similar.q: What are morals?
similar.a: rules that help us behave in ways that are appropriate, caring and thoughtful of others and ourselves

questions.q: When we want to control our emotions, it is good to speak in a loud voice.
why: The textbook says the opposite.
Say what you want to do in a **soft and low voice** (p. 2).
questions.tip: Self-control = calm: soft voice, no quick actions.

similar.q: True or false: self-control means avoiding quick actions.

questions.q: In the library drama, who showed self-control?
why: Semira shouted and came close to Rahel. Rahel answered with pride.
**Hagos** spoke calmly and admitted they were wrong (p. 6).
questions.tip: Look for the person who is calm and fair to both sides.

similar.q: What should Semira have done?
similar.a: told them politely to read quietly

questions.q: Our words are like ___. Once they are released, we can never get them back.
why: The story ends: "Our words are like feathers" (p. 8).
questions.tip: Feathers fly away in the wind and cannot be collected again.

similar.q: What do the holes in the fence stand for?
similar.a: the scars that angry words leave

questions.q: Jonas Salk refused to patent his vaccine because he wanted the whole world to benefit from it.
why: p. 9–10: he did not patent it. He wanted it provided to as many people as possible, for free.
questions.tip: Patent = only right to sell. Salk wanted it free.

similar.q: On whom did Salk first test his vaccine?
similar.a: himself, his wife and his three sons

questions.q: Self-control is what you do when ___.
why: p. 12: "Self-control is what you do when no one is watching."
If you behave only when adults are near, that is not consistent.
questions.tip: Think of the student who behaves "even when no one is looking" (p. 1).

similar.q: Consistency and ___ go hand in hand.

questions.q: Your thoughts affect your feelings. Your feelings affect your...
why: The self-control circle (p. 12): thoughts → feelings → decisions → actions.
questions.tip: Say the circle aloud: Think, Feel, Decide, Act.

similar.q: Why should you control your actions?
similar.a: because they can have serious consequences

questions.q: What were the consequences of the shepherd's lie?
questions.answer: When the hyena really came, the villagers did not believe him. The hyena killed many sheep. He lost the trust of all the villagers.
why: p. 13–14: the villagers laughed; many sheep died.
p. 16: he hurt himself because he lost the trust of the villagers.
questions.tip: Give two results: dead sheep and lost trust.

similar.q: Did the shepherd show respect to the villagers?
similar.a: No. He fooled them with false cries (p. 16).

questions.q: The student in "A Student Wanted!" says what when he has made a mistake?
why: p. 15: "when he/she has made a mistake says, 'I'm sorry'".
questions.tip: Match each sentence: don't know → "I don't know"; mistake → "I'm sorry"; task → "I'll do it".

similar.q: What does the wanted student say when he is asked to do a task?

units.intro: This unit is about the **power of education**, the qualities of a **good student**, **respect** at school, a good **study plan**, and the joy of **reading**.

cards.title: A cry for help (a story)
body: On an island lived many feelings: Happiness, Pride, Arrogance, Respect, Sadness, Love...
One day the island was going to **sink**. All the feelings left in their boats.
Only **Respect** stayed until the last moment. Then she asked for help.

cards.title: Who helps Respect?

states.label: Arrogance
states.text: **Arrogance**: "No. My boat is full of **gold and silver**. There is no place for you."

states.label: Pride
states.text: **Pride**: "I can't help you. You are **all wet** and might spoil my beautiful boat."

states.label: Sadness
states.text: **Sadness**: "I am so sorry. I need to be **by myself**."

states.label: Happiness
states.text: **Happiness** was so happy that she **did not even hear** Respect.

states.label: An elder
states.text: An **elder** said: "Come, Respect, I will take you." Later, Knowledge told Respect: it was **Education**.

body: Move the slider. Each boat passes by.

cards.title: The lesson of the story
body: Knowledge said: "Only **Education** is capable of understanding the greatness of **Respect**."
Education and respect go together.

cards.title: A proverb
body: "**Education is light; illiteracy is darkness.**"

cards.q: Why did Pride refuse to help Respect?

options.A: His boat was full of gold
options.B: Respect was wet and might spoil his boat

cards.why: Pride said: "You are all wet and might spoil my boat" (p. 19).

cards.title: Hassen's story
body: The textbook tells the story of **Hassen** in pictures, without words.
Look at each picture. What makes him a good student?

steps.text: Hassen is a student at **Kelhamet Junior School**.
He is **clean and well combed**.
He is **punctual**: always on time.
He does his **homework**.
He **washes his clothes**.
He **studies till late evening**.
He gets **good grades**.
He **helps in the farm**.
He **reads stories** to others.
He is **respected by elders**.

cards.title: Memory trick: a good student is good in 3 places

letters.m: helps in the farm, respected by elders

body: Think "**S-H-C**": **S**chool, **H**ome, **C**ommunity.

cards.q: The word "punctual" means...
cards.why: Hassen is punctual: he arrives on time (p. 20).

cards.title: Everyone at school is our teacher
body: A student says: "Our **director**, our school **guard**, the elderly mothers that **clean** our classes are all our teachers."
So greet them politely and offer help when they need it.

cards.title: Six ways to show respect
body: Tap the dots.

cards.title: More ways
body: - Pay attention and listen with interest.
- Write a note to a teacher: how much you enjoyed the lesson.
- Talk with classmates only when the teacher allows a group discussion.

cards.title: Ashebir, the troublesome student
body: Ashebir wastes time. He does not pay attention in class.
The teacher gave him advice. Ashebir gave the teacher a **bad look**.
The teacher sent him out and told him to bring his parents. It was the **second** time.

cards.title: Ashebir's mother
body: His **old mother** came. She looked sick and tired. She almost cried.
Ashebir **apologized** and promised not to do it again.
The teacher **forgave** him and explained respect to him.

cards.title: Respect elders, parents and teachers
body: It is our **culture** to respect our elders, family and teachers.
Always speak to them politely. Obey our parents. Never hurt their feelings.
Teachers give us a very special gift: **knowledge**. It makes us better people.

cards.title: Caught cheating
body: Four students played till late. They did not prepare for a test.
They made themselves dirty with grease. They lied: "The bus tyre burst. We pushed the bus."
The teacher gave them the test **three days later**, in **separate classrooms**.

cards.title: The teacher's test (100 marks)
head: Question
Marks
rows: What was the colour of the bus?

cards.title: How was the lie found?
body: The four students gave **different answers** to questions 2 and 3.
So the teacher understood that they tried to **cheat** him.

cards.title: A trip to the National Museum
body: The things in the museum are **old, fragile** and very **valuable**. They cannot be replaced.
The teacher said: "Do not touch anything."
**Himan** kept touching things. She even tried to touch the mummified bodies.
After many warnings, she was **sent out**. She learned: not respecting rules has **consequences**.

cards.title: Defacing school property
body: **Beyan** carved his name on a school bench with a stone. **Aron** wanted a turn.
The **guard** said: "You are defacing school property. You are responsible for the damage."
**Beyan** said: "The guard is right. We were wrong." **Aron** got angry and yelled.

cards.q: Why did the director forgive Beyan but not Aron?

options.A: Beyan did not carve the bench
options.B: Beyan accepted his mistake; Aron got angry and yelled

cards.why: The guard applauded Beyan for acknowledging his mistakes. Aron gave a mischievous look and yelled (p. 27).

cards.title: A good study plan
body: Good students need a good **study plan** for their lessons.
They know what to do **before** class, **in** class and **after** class.

cards.title: Three times to be a good student

steps.text: **Before class**: prepare well. Read the textbook. Prepare ahead for the next class.
**In class**: listen attentively and participate.
**After class**: work hard and study your lessons.

cards.title: Good in all three
body: Good in class but lazy after class? **Not** a good student.
Works hard at home but does not listen in class? **Not** a good student.
A good student is good **before, in and after** class.

cards.title: Some things to do (Activity 2.3)
body: **In class**:
- raise your hand to ask, take notes,
- focus on the teacher, listen to classmates' questions,
- give your opinion in discussion.
**Before class**: do the assignments, prepare questions, read the textbook.
**After class**: do homework right away, go through your notes, write questions for next class.

cards.title: My daily timetable
body: Draw a **seven-day** timetable, from 06:00 to 24:00.
Colour each activity with its own colour.

cards.title: The colour key
body: Each activity has a colour.

cards.title: Check your timetable
body: Do you spend enough time on **studying**, **relaxing** and **physical activities**?
Plan your week to spread your activities **evenly**.

cards.q: In the timetable, which colour is for study?
cards.why: Study (homework and school projects) is blue (p. 29).

lessons.title: She or he who reads blossoms

cards.title: Read more than textbooks
body: Reading textbooks alone is **not enough**.
A good student also reads **other books**.

cards.title: Alemseged Tesfai
body: **Alemseged Tesfai** is a well-known writer in Eritrea.
He believes the secret of his writing was that he was a **good reader**.
He wrote: "**A good book is as good a companion as your best friend.**"

cards.title: Why do we read?
body: We read to study or prepare for an exam. We read for our job.
But the **greatest pleasure and benefit** comes from other kinds of reading.

cards.title: Six kinds of reading
body: Tap the dots.

cards.title: What reading gives you
body: Your knowledge grows. Your **lessons become easier**. It helps you build your **career**.
The best time to start a **reading habit** is when you are **young**.

cards.title: Kalulu the Hare
body: In grade six, his brother bought him a book: "**Kalulu the Hare**", about a hare.
He liked it so much that he read it again. He has never stopped reading.
Today he rarely sleeps without reading a few pages. Reading helped him become a **writer**.

cards.title: Summary: why education?
body: Education helps us **understand our environment, society and the world**.
If we know them better, we will be **respected** and **successful**.
We learn at school, but also from our **families**, **friends**, while **travelling** and in many other places.
People who changed the world were **educated**.

cards.title: Respect yourself
body: Take care of three things.

cards.title: Three kinds of respect

body: **Sharing** is an important part of life. Visitors are always welcome to stay and eat.

steps.text: Everyone **washes their hands** before eating.
They sit in a **circle** on large mats. A huge dish is in the middle.
Each person eats from the part of the dish **in front of him or her**. Reaching across the dish is very bad manners!
Only the **right hand** is used for eating. Do not lean on your left hand.
We usually **don't talk** while eating. Talking shows a lack of respect for the food.
Everybody washes hands **by age**: father first, then mother, then the others. A younger child passes the water dish and earns blessings. A **visitor** washes first.
Father makes us say a **prayer**.
Father **blesses the bread** and offers a piece to each person.
After eating, everyone washes again **in the same order**.
**Mother and the young ones** clean the table.

steps.text: **Afa**, a farmer near **Tesenai**, has six children. They do not want to work. Now Afa is old and very ill.

units.intro: This unit is about **oppression** in the world, famous **revolutions**, and the **Eritrean Revolution**: its start, the Strategic Withdrawal, the 6th Offensive and the **Tegadalai**.

pins.text: oppression: discrimination against a group of people

cards.title: What is oppression?
body: **Oppression** is discrimination against a **group** of people.
In history there have been many kinds of oppression.

cards.title: Three kinds in this lesson
body: Tap the dots.

cards.title: Oppression of women
body: For most of history, women had very few rights.
People thought women were naturally weaker than men, in body and mind. So women were treated unfairly.
**Gender discrimination** happens in jobs, education, courts and politics.

cards.title: Women in our society
body: In our society women were not seen as equal to men. They were treated as **second class** members.
Girls were not given education. They were expected to stay at home.

cards.title: Colonialism
body: Europe colonized **Africa, Latin America and Asia** for centuries.
Europeans saw the riches of Africa. They took control of the people and imposed their rule. This is **colonialism**.
The only reason for colonialism in Africa was **exploitation**: taking Africa's resources by force.

cards.title: Slavery
body: European traders first found spices and gold in West Africa. Later they sold people as **slaves**.
Between the **17th and 19th centuries**, about **20 million** people were sold as slaves to colonists in America.
Slaves worked on **sugar and cotton** plantations. They were not paid.

cards.q: What was the only reason for colonialism in Africa, according to the textbook?
cards.why: The colonizers took Africa's resources by force: exploitation (p. 48).

cards.title: Oppression brings struggle
body: Where there is oppression, there is often **struggle**.
**Revolution** was the most common form of struggle against colonialism.
Revolutions bring big changes in **power, culture, economy** and **institutions**.

cards.title: The Haitian Revolution
body: Started in **1791**. It was **against slavery**, led by the slaves against the **French** colonialists.
By 1792 the slaves controlled a third of the island. France gave civil and political rights.
In **1804** Haiti became **independent**.

cards.title: The Algerian Revolution
body: Algeria was a colony of **France**. The French colonial government was violent.
The **National Liberation Front (FLN)** led the struggle.
After **eight years** and **one million** deaths, Algeria became independent in **July 1962**.

cards.title: The French Revolution
body: Most people in France were poor peasants or workers. Taxes were high and food was expensive.
Society was divided: a **few rich** and **many poor**.
In **1789** the people overthrew **King Louis XVI**. The monarchy ended and a **republic** began.

cards.title: Memory trick: the French goals
body: "**E**very **F**rench **L**ife": Equality, Fraternity, Liberty.

steps.text: **1789**: the French Revolution.
**1791**: the Haitian Revolution against slavery.
**1804**: Haiti is independent.
**July 1962**: Algeria is independent.

cards.q: Which revolution was led by slaves against the French?
cards.why: The Haitian Revolution of 1791 was against slavery, led by the slaves (p. 49).

cards.title: Eritrea and colonialism
body: Like most of Africa, Eritrea was a victim of **colonialism**.
Eritreans won over colonialism after **thirty years of Armed Struggle**.

steps.text: **Turkey**
**Egypt**
**Italy**
**Britain**
**Ethiopia**: Eritreans fought a 30-year armed struggle against Ethiopian colonialism.
In **May 1991** Eritrea finally became **independent**.

cards.title: Memory trick: the five powers
body: "**T**he **E**agle **I**s **B**ack **E**ast": Turkey, Egypt, Italy, Britain, Ethiopia.

Answer

cards.title: A resilient struggle
body: The Eritrean armed struggle was **resilient**.
It won after overcoming **many challenges**. That makes it unique.
"**The beginning is always difficult.**" The first fighters started without enough people and supplies.

cards.title: By 1977, most of Eritrea was free
body: The **EPLF** liberated Qarora, Nakfa, Afabet, Dekemhare, Keren, Segeneyti and part of Massawa.
The **ELF** liberated Tessenei, Mendefera, Adi Quala and Aqurdet.
Asmara was surrounded. Independence was very close.

cards.title: Then the balance changed
body: The **Soviet Union** gave massive military help to the **Dergue** regime in Ethiopia.
So the EPLF decided to leave these places and go back to **Sahil**.
On the way, it fought and weakened the enemy and protected civilians (victories at Elabered and Maemide).
This is the **Strategic Withdrawal of 1978**.

cards.title: Which road?

states.label: Defend at all cost
states.text: "Defending the liberated areas **at all cost**." But fighting a huge force face to face would weaken the fighters. It would put the revolution in danger.

states.label: Withdraw
states.text: "Reserving man power and logistics, **withdraw and reorganize**": the EPLF chose this road. One step backward, two steps forward.

body: The picture shows two roads. Move the slider.

cards.title: Yemane explains with a sack

states.label: All at once
states.text: A 50 kilo sack is too heavy. If Geled tries to carry it at once, he will **hurt his back**. Then he cannot even lift 10 kilos.

states.label: Five parts
states.text: Divide it into **five parts of 10 kilos** and carry them in five rounds. That is what the fighters did: withdraw, stay strong, and win later.

body: Move the slider.

head: The Dergue had...
The fighters had...

no one: "we were all by ourselves"

cards.title: One step backward, two steps forward
body: Withdrawing was a **wise decision**. It needed courage and confidence to start again.
This **resilience** led to victory in the end.

cards.title: The 6th Offensive ("Red Star")
body: The **6th Offensive**, also called the **Red Star Campaign**, was the biggest and hardest Ethiopian offensive.
Before it, **five** offensives were carried out between July 1978 and July 1979. They failed.
The 6th took **two years** to prepare. It started on **15 February 1982** and went on for **95 days**.

cards.title: Two armies
body: Tap the dots.

cards.title: The enemy's side
body: The goal: to destroy the Eritrean revolution once and for all.
Ethiopia had the full support of the **Soviet Union** and an alliance with **Libya** and **South Yemen**.
It used the prohibited **GA nerve poison gas** against the fighters.

cards.title: Bdho = Challenge
body: The Eritrean answer was "**Bdho**", meaning "**Challenge**".
A famous slogan: "Lomi zeyketete bdewu kem zmote": "**Every one shall fight or fall where he stands**."
A famous song of the time: "Bdho" by **Estifanos Abraham (Zemach)**.

cards.title: "Red Star Sets"
body: The magazine **The Economist** (15 May 1982) wrote that the offensive **failed**.
Its main aim, the capture of **Nakfa**, was not achieved. The EPLF was not crushed.

cards.title: The Tegadalai
body: At the core of this resilience is the **Tegadalai**. Tap the dots.

cards.title: A letter of a martyr
body: Martyr **Haile Tewelde** and two comrades were hanged by the Dergue in **Asseb** on **3 April 1976**.
In his last hours he wrote to his mother: "Don't cry or feel sad for me. That is what our enemy wants."
"I am dying for my country and people... **Eritrea will never perish**."

cards.title: What his letter shows
body: Activity 4.3 asks how Haile shows six qualities. Tap the dots.

cards.title: Who were the victims?
body: Oppression targets groups: **women**, people of a certain caste, religion, tribe, clan or nationality, **slaves**, **colonized people**.

body: **Ibrahim** lived in refugee camps in **Sudan**. He came home in **1992**, after the war, when Eritrea was free.

"With our blood and our vote, freedom has been realized. Hail, hail, Eritrea, your flag is hoisted... Rest in peace our martyrs."

cards.title: Blood and vote
body: **Blood**: the armed struggle and the martyrs.
**Vote**: the referendum, when the people chose freedom.

cards.title: Why a referendum?
body: **President Issaias Afwerki**: international recognition can only come through a **democratic and legal** end to the conflict. So the EPLF showed the **free and fair choice** of the people through a referendum.

cards.title: The last chapter
body: **Dr Amare Tekle**, Commissioner of the Referendum Commission: the referendum was the **last, political chapter** of the struggle.
The people used their right to **self-determination**, denied for over 30 years.

steps.text: Eritreans **vote** in the referendum.
International representatives **observe** the vote (UNOVER).
On **Tuesday 27 April 1993**, **Mr. Samir Sanbar**, the UN Secretary-General's Special Representative, says the referendum was **free and fair** at every stage.
Eritrea officially **declares its independence** on **24 May 1993**.

body: **1991 = freedom won. 1993 = independence declared** (24 May).

lessons.title: The structure and function of the Eritrean Government

cards.title: Three branches
body: Tap the dots.

steps.text: **Legislative**: the **National Assembly** elects the **President** from among its members, by an absolute majority.
The National Assembly also **passes laws** and oversees their execution, based on the constitution.
**Executive**: the **President** makes the final decisions on government policies, with the **cabinet**.
The **Ministers** direct, supervise and coordinate the affairs of the government.
**Judiciary**: the **Supreme Court** is the only body that can **interpret the constitution**. It also interprets laws and settles disputes.
**Lower Courts** settle disputes based on the law.

lessons.title: The Boat, the Camel and the Shop

cards.title: Three secret patriots
body: **Ami Hamoda**, **Yba Sfaf** and **Yma Juket** were members of the **Hafash wdubat**.
They did not know each other's real names. They had **code names** from the EPLF **Jemahir** of zoba Mbraq.

cards.title: The supply chain

steps.text: **The Boat** brings food and other items from **Yemen**.
He hides them in the **Shawra trees** off the seashore. He loads and unloads **alone, at night**.
**The Camel** loads his camel. He walks from Gedem to the coast of **Zula** (near ancient **Adulis**), and on to Shieb, **at night**.
**The Shop** in **Shieb** keeps the arrivals and departures of the camel **secret**.
From Shieb, the fighters carry the things to their bases in **Selemuna**.

body: This picture is a simple plan, not a real map.

cards.title: Why so secret?
body: Their main fear was **not** being killed.
They were careful so they would **not endanger the supply route** of the fighters.
These **selfless** patriots worked with determination until **Independence Day**.

cards.q: What was the main fear of the Boat, the Camel and the Shop?

cards.why: Their utmost care was not to endanger the supply route of the fighters (p. 88).

**Samira** wants to be a doctor. Her models are the doctors of the armed struggle.
She read "**The Journey from Nakfa to Nakfa**" by **Dr. Tekeste Fikadu**, about the EPLF medical staff.

cards.title: Sirro

His model is **Daniel Teklehaimanot**, the best African sportsman of **2012**.
Daniel was champion of Africa for **three years in a row**.

cards.title: Eritrea resisted many rulers
body: The people of Eritrea resisted many foreign rules:
the **Turkish**, the **Egyptians**, the **Tigryan chiefs**, the **Italians**, the **British**.
Finally they defeated **Ethiopian** colonial rule and won independence.

steps.text: Zemat was the **Nebtab** (chief of the Tigre people in Barka) of the village **Ad-Ali Bekit** in Barka-la'lay.
He led a small traditional army of the **Reb'at**. He defended his people from the **Mahdists** (from the Sudan) and the **Tigryan chiefs**.
When the **Italians** came, he refused foreign rule. He attacked Italian soldiers in Barka-la'lay.
He was a famous **poet and orator**. His poem says: "Who are those strangers?... It is not us but them who should pay the taxes."
The Italians took him to **Nakura island prison**. He died there with other patriots.
His people loved him. Ad-Ali Bekit is now called **Ad-Zemat** in his honour.

cards.title: What is the Reb'at?
body: **Reb'at** is a social organization of the **youth** of the Tigre people.
Its young people are the **defenders of the land** and **enforcers of the law** in traditional Tigre society.

cards.q: Where did Zemat wed Ekud die?
cards.why: The Italians took him to Nakura island prison, where he died (p. 91).

cards.title: A symbol of identity
body: The **national flag** is one of the **symbols of national identity**.
It is a sign of **independence**. It symbolizes **patriotism** and the nation's endowments.

cards.title: Beautiful colours (a story)
body: At **6 P.M.** a mother walks with her children on **Harnet Avenue**, Asmara.
She hears a whistle: the flag is being lowered. She stands at attention. Drivers stop and get out of their cars.
It reminds her of the **big price** paid to see this flag fly.

cards.title: What made her sad
body: **Two young men** at the bus station kept sitting and chatting. They did not take off their hats.
But her **daughter** took off her hat and told her little brother to do the same.

cards.title: Our flag and its design
body: Our flag is a symbol of our **history** and our **future**.
Its basic design comes from the flag of the **EPLF**.

cards.title: Look at the flag
body: Tap the dots to see each part.

cards.title: Remember the design
body: **Two triangles** in green and blue, and a **red triangle** pointing away from the hoist side.
In the red triangle: **golden olive branches**. They come from the **1952** Eritrean flag and symbolize **peace**.

cards.title: "Who am I?" (a poem)
body: "I am recognized all over the world... In school you raise me up every morning, take me down every evening. You don't let me touch the ground, and you fold me with respect."
Who am I? The **flag**!

cards.q: Where do the olive branches on our flag come from?
cards.why: The olive branches were taken from the 1952 Eritrean flag; they symbolize peace (p. 98).

cards.title: Two special days
body: Tap the dots.

steps.text: **Sara**: two of her children were martyred. Her granddaughter serves in the Air Force. May 24 reminds her to be a **proud Eritrean**.
**Ali**: Independence Day should be **honoured and celebrated every year**. Promise to contribute to development.
**Abrham**: the celebrations show **nationalism, unity, comradeship, heroism**. A time to learn about the revolution.
**Zahra**: we should be **thankful every day**, not only one day a year.
**Bekit**: enjoys the festivities and celebrates freedom with **thankfulness**.
**Nejat**: after independence in 1991, "we still had to fight **another war** to defend our freedom". "We never kneel down."

cards.title: What the voices share
body: May 24 is a day to be **proud** and **thankful**.
It is a day to **remember** the sacrifice and **promise** to help build Eritrea.

cards.title: Stand up for our martyrs (a poem)
body: "Light the candles. Everyone please stand up. Take off the hat and scarf. **Bow your head for one minute**..."
"We vow to double our efforts... Rest in peace our martyrs."

steps.text: An Eritrean youth sees an old black plastic sandal, a **shida**, on her aunt's wall. Before independence, her aunt walked from her village to **Asmara**.
One day she heard a battle in the mountains. She **hid in a cave**.
She saw soldiers dragging a **wounded Eritrean fighter**. One of his shoes slipped off.
Later she picked up the shoe and **hung it** in her home.
She keeps it in memory of **all** the fighters. Her **three sons** also died in the war.

cards.title: June 20: Martyrs' Day
body: **June 20** is a national holiday to pay tribute to all who died for the nation's freedom.
On the eve: **candle lighting** and **prayer services**.
We also **renew our pledge** to help build our nation.

steps.text: Over **65,000**, mostly young men and women, in the 30-year war of liberation. Freedom became real in 1991.
Seven years later, **20,000** more died defending that freedom.
Over **85,000** in all: every Eritrean family lost at least a son, daughter or close relative.

cards.title: The She'eb massacre
body: She'eb is a village in the **eastern lowlands**.
The enemy had a great defeat at the **Battle of Afabet**. Then Ethiopian soldiers turned their guns on the defenceless civilians of She'eb.
Over **400** villagers, including children, were shot dead and wounded.

cards.title: We remember
body: Today a **Martyrs' monument** in She'eb remembers the massacre of **12 May 1988**. The names are written on marble.
Sacrifices were made not only in the hills but also in our **villages, towns and cities**.
Our task: remember our martyrs, and **build a free and just society**.

units.title: Our Acts and their Consequences: Right and Wrong
units.intro: This unit is about how to choose **right** from **wrong**, what a **wrongful act** is (deliberate or careless), and the **consequences** of our acts.

pins.text: Deep down in my heart, how do I feel about it?
Could it hurt anyone, including me?
How would I feel if somebody did it to me?
Have I ever been told that it is wrong?
How will I feel later if I do it?
What would adults I respect say about it?
Still not sure? Talk to someone you trust and respect.

decide.title: How to make the right decision

pins.text: you are not sure what to do
yes: consult family and adults, watch good adults, read
no time: ask yourself about rightness, fairness and consequences
then decide; do not act in haste

cards.title: Choices
body: Some choices are not serious: a blue or a yellow trouser?
Other choices are between **right and wrong**. Sometimes it is not easy to know what to do.

cards.title: Stop and think!
body: Whenever you are not sure what is right: **stop and think!**

cards.title: Nine questions to ask yourself
body: Tap each dot.

cards.title: Three students talk
body: **Thomas** decides at once, but later he often feels sorry.
**Merriam** says that is wrong. She consults elders: older brothers and sisters, and her **parents** for serious issues.

cards.title: Why do the right thing when it is hard?
body: Doing only what suits us, without caring about others' rights, can make us **selfish** or **irresponsible**.
We should do right and useful things that benefit **us and the society**, even if they are hard.

steps.text: You are not sure what is right.
Do you have time?
**Yes**: consult family and other adults. Watch adults and learn from their good behaviour. **Reading** also gives experience.
**No time**: at least ask yourself about the **rightness**, **fairness** and **possible consequences**.
Then decide. **Hasty decisions and acts are usually risky.**

cards.title: What would you do? (Activity 8.1)
body: - An empty old house has a "**Do not enter!**" sign, but the door is open. No one is around.
- Kids make fun of another kid. They call you a coward if you don't join.
- You are hungry and pass a **farm full of fruit**. No one is looking.
- A friend asks you to help him **cheat** on a test.

cards.q: You pass a farm full of fruit. No one is looking. Is taking fruit right?

options.A: Yes, a few fruits do no harm
options.B: Yes, if no one is looking
options.C: No: taking what is not yours is theft, an illegal act

cards.why: Theft is an illegal act by its nature (p. 115). Ask: "Would it violate any rule? How would I feel if somebody did it to me?" (p. 110).

cards.title: "Golden advice"
body: A school director and parents gave this advice:
- **Think twice before acting once.**
- Think about how your actions affect the people around you.
- Within society, **laws** define what acts are wrong. Know the laws and rules, and you are on the safe side.

cards.title: It's never okay to do the wrong thing
body: Ask yourself the questions. Consult people you trust. Follow the rules.

cards.q: Rahwa says hasty decisions and acts are usually...
cards.why: "You should not act in haste. Hasty decisions and acts are usually risky" (p. 112).

cards.title: Definition
body: A **wrongful act** is committed when someone **deliberately** or **carelessly** causes **harm or loss** to another person or property.

cards.title: Right act and wrong act
body: A court official, **Ato Abraham**, explains:
Doing things according to the rules, laws, custom and morals is the **right act**.
Doing things against them makes the person **responsible**. This is a **wrongful act**, or "**wrong**".

steps.text: **Deliberate**: done on purpose. Theft, killing (murder) and insult are illegal by their nature.
**Careless**: a lawful act done without proper care. Example: riding a bike or driving a car without care for people on the road.
Both can cause **harm or loss** to a person or property.
The law says: the wrongdoer should **compensate** the victim for the harm, damage or loss.

cards.title: What if the wrongdoer is a child?
body: If a child under the control of parents causes harm, usually the **parents** are responsible, or pay the compensation.
So we cannot escape by saying "I am a child". Young people may also be punished themselves, but not in the same way as adults.

cards.title: Plaintiff and defendant
body: Tap the dots.

cards.title: Memory trick
body: **P**laintiff = **P**ain (suffered harm). **D**efendant = **D**id it.

cards.title: The broken window (a dialogue)
body: Abraham and friends played **volleyball in the corridor**. They broke a window. The director called their parents.
Salih: "It was an accident. Is it fair to punish him?"
Tesfu: "A person is also responsible for a **careless** act, even if he did not mean to cause harm."

cards.title: How and where to play

states.label: In the corridor
states.text: Playing in corridors, classrooms and halls is **wrong** by itself. And the ball was kicked carelessly.

states.label: On the playground
states.text: School rules say: play only on the **playing grounds**. "It is not only **how** to play, but also **where** to play." Rules are for our **safety**.

cards.title: More case stories (Activity 8.6)
body: - **Aboy Abdela** put a hard-to-see wire across his garden. **Haben** rode his bike through, fell and lost two teeth.
- **Hayelom**, 10, pulled a chair away from **Adey Zemzem** as a joke. She fell and was seriously hurt.
- At a party, **Hana** gave beer to two 14-year-olds. **Samuel** rode his bike and injured an old man.
- **Bereket** and friends played football in the street. A ball struck an old woman.
The textbook asks: who is responsible, and why?

cards.title: Summary
body: Our actions have **consequences**, and we are **responsible** for them.
Society requires us to **compensate** anyone we injure because we failed to act in the required way.

cards.q: Who is the plaintiff?

options.B: the person who suffered injury or loss

cards.why: The person who suffers injury, loss or damage is the plaintiff; the wrongdoer is the defendant (p. 116).

tips.text: Learn the definition word by word: "deliberately **or** carelessly causes harm or loss to another person or property".
Deliberate = **planned** / on purpose. Careless = **no proper care** (speeding, playing in the corridor, ignoring warnings).
Plaintiff = was hurt. Defendant = did the wrong.
"Choose the best answer" questions in this unit often end with "**all of the above**" or "a & b".

questions.q: How can you decide whether some actions are right or wrong?

options.A: ask if it could hurt anyone

why: p. 110: ask "Could it hurt anyone?"

questions.tip: All three are in the unit.

similar.q: Name one question to ask yourself before acting.
similar.a: Is it fair? (or Could it hurt anyone? Would it violate any rule?)

questions.q: One of the following is a benefit of doing the right thing.
why: Punishment is a result of wrong acts, not a benefit.
Peace of mind and satisfaction are benefits.
questions.tip: Remove the bad option, then look for "a & b".

similar.q: How does Thomas feel after deciding in haste?

questions.q: Identify the possible consequence of wrongful acts.
why: Wrongdoers must compensate and may be punished (p. 115–116).
They may also feel bad later ("How will I feel later if I do it?", p. 110).
questions.tip: Every option is a bad result → "all".

similar.q: What should a wrongdoer pay to the victim?

questions.q: A wrongful act is committed when someone deliberately or ___ causes harm or loss to another person or property.
why: p. 115 definition.
questions.tip: Two ways: deliberately or carelessly.

similar.q: Give one example of an act that is illegal by its nature.

questions.q: In a case, the person who suffers injury or loss because of another's wrong is the:
why: p. 116: the one who suffers is the plaintiff; the wrongdoer is the defendant.
questions.tip: P = pain.

similar.q: What is the wrongdoer called?

questions.q: Asmerom hid in the dark and attacked Berhe with a hard stick. Earlier he said, "I will punish Berhe tonight." Deliberate or careless? Why?
questions.answer: Deliberate. He planned it and said so before; he wanted to cause harm.
why: A deliberate act is done on purpose.
His words show a plan.
questions.tip: Look for a plan or a wish to harm.

similar.q: Sherif rode very fast near a school and hit a child. Deliberate or careless?
similar.a: careless: he did not keep the speed limit

questions.q: Abraham is not responsible for the broken window because he did not break it on purpose.
why: p. 117: a person is also responsible for a careless act, even without the intention to cause harm.
Also, playing in the corridor is against school rules.
questions.tip: Careless acts are wrongs too.

similar.q: Where should students play, according to the school rules?

questions.q: Why should a person be responsible for his or her actions?
questions.answer: Because our actions have consequences for other people and property. The law says a person who causes harm must compensate the victim, and being responsible stops us from being selfish.
why: p. 122 summary: we are responsible for the consequences.
p. 116: compensation.
questions.tip: Actions → consequences → responsibility.

similar.q: Who usually pays if a child causes harm?

questions.q: How can wrongful acts affect society?
questions.answer: They cause harm or loss to people and property (injuries, damaged things), put families in trouble, and break the laws that keep society safe.
why: p. 115, 121–122: harm to persons and property; fires spreading to neighbours; injuries on the road.
questions.tip: Use an example from the case stories.

similar.q: How many huts did Mahmud's fire destroy?

questions.q: In a case about a wrongful act, the wrongdoer is called the defendant.
why: p. 116: the one who suffers is the plaintiff; the wrongdoer is the defendant.
questions.tip: D = the one who did it.

similar.q: Who is the plaintiff?
similar.a: the person who suffered injury, loss or damage

units.title: Being an Active Citizen
units.intro: This unit is about **kindness**, being a **good and active citizen** (paying taxes, keeping the environment clean, helping the police), and the **three types of citizens**.

pins.text: services: public hospitals, free public schools, teachers' pay
the criminal is corrected and learns
the community benefits: crime may not happen again
what happens to your neighbour today may happen to you tomorrow

cards.title: A lost transport fee
body: A boy lost the money his mother gave him for **transport**. He noticed when he wanted to pay.
A **woman** saw he was worried. She **paid the fee** for him.
He said "Thank you very much", but he did not ask her name or address.

cards.title: How can he repay her?
body: The son wants to do something good for the woman in return.
His mother says: it is good to do good for those who help us.
But it is **more important** to show kindness to **other people**.

cards.title: Kindness is not like borrowed money
body: Borrowed money is given back to the same person. Kindness is different.
**Kindness is learned from the kind acts of others.**
By being kind, you **teach others** to be kind.

cards.title: Watch kindness grow

states.label: Step 1
states.text: The woman is kind to the boy.

states.label: Step 2
states.text: The boy learns and is kind to **other people**.

states.label: Step 3
states.text: They learn too, and are kind to others. **Kindness is multiplied!**

body: Move the slider.

cards.title: A good culture
body: The mother says: "There are many kind people in our country. We are proud that we have a good **culture of helping each other**."

cards.q: How do we multiply kindness?

options.A: by being kind only to those who are kind to us
options.B: by being kind to other people, after learning from others' kindness
options.C: by paying it back like money

cards.why: We multiply kindness by being kind to other people; we learn to be kind from the kindness of others (p. 125, Exercise 9.1).

cards.title: Active citizens solve problems
body: As citizens we can solve the problems of our communities **if we are active citizens**.
Example: "I am a responsible and active citizen because I put trash in a garbage container."

cards.title: A shopkeeper's story
body: **Semere** helps in his parents' shop. He always respects the law and advises people who break it.
He learned that the government gives services to citizens with the help of **tax**.

cards.title: What is a tax?
body: A **tax** is money paid to the government from the **income** of citizens.
The government provides services using taxpayers' money.
A **receipt** is a printed paper that shows the amount paid to the seller.

steps.text: Citizens earn an **income**.
They pay **tax**. Sellers must give **receipts**.
The **government** collects the tax.
It pays for **services**: public hospitals, free public schools, and teachers' salaries.

cards.title: Semere corrects his father
body: His father did not give receipts to customers: he cheated on tax.
Semere: "You tell me not to cheat in exams. Cheating the government is not different!"
His father stopped. Semere **applied what he learned at school**.

cards.title: The football field
body: Some households threw **garbage** on the open field where young people played football. It smelled bad.

cards.title: What the young people did

states.label: The problem
states.text: Garbage on the field. A **bad smell**.

states.label: The campaign
states.text: First they **informed the administrator**. Then they cleaned the field. The administrator supported them and advised residents to use the container.

states.label: The result
states.text: The administrator bought them a **nice ball**. Residents promised to keep the area clean. No more bad smell.

body: Move the slider.

cards.title: A thief and the police
body: Aman stole money from **Mama Halima's** house. The police are looking for him.
**Daniel** first did not want to help: "He was a nice person."
**Fars** and **Senai** ask: "What if the old woman was your own mother?"

cards.title: Why help the police?
body: Tap the dots.

cards.title: Your neighbour today, you tomorrow
body: If a thief is not punished today, he will be encouraged to steal more.
